query: The Wind in the Slits {The wind plays the seventh tower's arrow-slits like a flute, a different note at every window.|The tower is playing again. You'd swear the tune has more notes than there are windows.|The wind's song. You can hum the first part now; nobody else in the castle knows it.} {Today it sounds almost like a lullaby.|Today it is quick and fretful, as if late for something.|{season == "winter": It plays low and slow, like something under snow.|It plays in fits, between gusts.}} Hum along and listen {You hum back. For a moment the tower answers in harmony, and the air goes thin and bright, and you come away drained and happy, as after a long song.|You hum, and one window falls silent as if to listen. It costs you something to keep going. You keep going.|You hum the part you know and the tower plays the rest. When it's done your hands are cold to the elbow and you're smiling.} Write the tune down {You mark each window's note in your notebook. It's a scale nobody uses any more; you find it later in a very old songbook.|You write the notes down and get a different tune each time you read them back. That seems important, and you can't think why.|Your page of notes is filling up. The tune has the same shape as the stair, you realise; you climb it, more or less.}
